note: GENERATED — edit tools/gen-glossary.cjs, not this file. `usage` is measured against src/content/data/*.json at build time so the numbers cannot go stale.

terms.first_use_explanation: Answering with text fetched at query time instead of text baked into the weights.
One indexable piece of a source document — the unit retrieval returns.
terms.note: `trozo` is NOT banned: its 5 uses mean an ordinary piece — "un trozo de residuo (cruft)", "un trozo de pegamento" — never a retrieval chunk.

terms.first_use_explanation: Splitting source documents into indexable pieces; size and boundaries decide what can be found.
terms.note: `trozeo` was added after the scanner's FILES list was fixed to include builds.json: a build challenge ships "pipeline de trozeo y embebido", and the gate had reported 0 occurrences because it was not reading that file. A ban list is only as wide as the corpus it is checked against.

terms.first_use_explanation: Repeating the tail of one chunk at the head of the next, so a fact spanning a boundary survives.
A vector placed so that distance between two vectors tracks similarity of meaning.
Reordering retrieved candidates with a slower, more accurate model before the generator reads them.
A lexical ranking function: scores a document by how often the query's exact terms appear in it.
A layered proximity graph for approximate nearest-neighbour search; trades recall for query speed.
How many retrieved results are passed on. Raising it costs context and can add noise.
The fraction of the relevant documents that actually came back. It bounds what the generator can use.
terms.note: Neither `recuerdo` nor `exhaustividad` is banned, and both were until the scanner's file list was widened. `recuerdo` reads as 'memory' — its one use is "recuerdo difuso sobre episodios", about agent memory — and `exhaustividad` means exhaustiveness ("abdicación disfrazada de exhaustividad"). Neither is the metric this term names.

terms.first_use_explanation: The share of queries whose answer appears anywhere in what was retrieved.
The whole body of documents available to retrieve from, at the moment of the query.
Tying each claim in an answer to a passage that was actually retrieved.
terms.note: `fundamentación` (5) edges out `grounding` (3); both are thin, and the Spanish form wins on evidence.

terms.first_use_explanation: A metric suite for retrieval pipelines — faithfulness, context precision, answer relevance.
The index that holds embeddings and answers nearest-neighbour queries over them.
terms.note: Both `vector store` (4) and `almacén de vectores` (3) ship; the English form wins as canonical.

terms.first_use_explanation: Fetching candidate passages for a query, before any generation happens.
terms.note: Spanish overwhelmingly says `recuperación` (299 vs 38). `búsqueda` is NOT banned — it means lookup.

terms.first_use_explanation: Running lexical and vector retrieval together and fusing the two ranked lists.
Whether the generated answer is supported by the retrieved context and nothing else.
The full text the model reads before producing a token — instructions, context and question.
The unit a model reads and emits — a few characters, not a word. What you are billed for.
terms.note: The auth sense (`signed token`) is the same word and equally kept.

terms.first_use_explanation: A model that predicts the next token over text, used here as a component with a cost and a failure mode.
Updating the model's weights on curated examples to change behaviour, not to add facts.
terms.note: `fine-tuning` dominates 106 to 3. The two remaining `ajuste fino` uses are inside book and article titles being cited, which is why the phrase itself is not banned.

terms.first_use_explanation: Fine-tuning by training small added matrices instead of the full weights, so it fits on one GPU.
Scales the logits before sampling; near zero sharpens toward the single most likely token.
terms.note: Spanish keeps the English word for the sampling parameter to avoid reading as physical heat.

terms.first_use_explanation: The keys and values of already-processed tokens, held in GPU memory so each new token is cheap.
An open JSON-RPC protocol standardising how a host application connects a model to tools and resources.
The model emitting a structured request for a function the application then runs.
terms.note: Only 5 uses; `llamado de herramientas` appears once and is banned to settle the inconsistency.

terms.first_use_explanation: Serving several requests in one forward pass, trading a little latency for much more throughput.
terms.note: `lotes` / `por lotes` also ship (60 uses) and are accepted in prose; the noun is `batching`.

terms.first_use_explanation: Storing weights or cache at lower precision to fit more model in the same memory.
The maximum number of tokens the model can read in one call.
Constraining generation so the result parses as a declared schema.
Running the model to produce output, as opposed to training it.
Operating a model behind an endpoint: batching, queueing, autoscaling and the tail latency it produces.
terms.note: Inconsistent (14 vs 56). `inferencia` and `servir` are NOT banned — both are correct in their own senses.

terms.first_use_explanation: A fixed labelled set a change is scored against, so a regression is a number rather than an opinion.
terms.note: Spanish says `evaluación` (188) far more than `eval` (66); `eval` survives in fixed phrases like `eval set`.

terms.first_use_explanation: How many calls the system completes per unit of time.
terms.note: `rendimiento` is banned because it also means performance in general, which loses the distinction from latency.

terms.first_use_explanation: A hard time limit on a remote call; without one, a slow dependency holds your threads.
A signal that propagates "I am full, slow down" upstream instead of buffering silently.
terms.note: `contrapresión` (4) is a real Spanish word for this and is allowed; `presión inversa` is the calque.

terms.first_use_explanation: A client-side switch that stops sending traffic to a dependency after a failure threshold.
terms.note: `cortacircuitos` (3) is the standard Spanish electrical term and reads naturally; only the word-by-word calque is banned.

terms.first_use_explanation: Deliberately rejecting or degrading a fraction of requests fast when over capacity.
terms.note: Narrowly prefers `descarte de carga` (8 vs 7). `alivio de carga` is NOT banned — it means relief, as in "a cache buys load relief, not correctness".

terms.first_use_explanation: A degraded answer served when a dependency is down — a cached value, a default, a partial page.
Promoting a follower to leader when the leader dies. Writes pause while it happens.
One partition of the data, owned by an independent primary.
Splitting rows across independent primaries so write load divides too.
Giving each tenant a random subset of workers, so one bad tenant rarely shares all of yours.
terms.note: Only 3 Spanish uses against 14 English, but there is no Spanish rendering at all — the technique has no established translation, so the English name is kept.

terms.first_use_explanation: A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions, used when one atomic transaction is impossible.
Writing the event into the same transaction as the data, then publishing it from that table.
Durability by appending the change to a log before applying it, so a crash can replay.
Where a message goes after it has failed enough times to stop being retried.
The extra latency of the first call into a function that has no warm instance.
terms.note: Spanish prefers `arranque en frío` (10 vs 7), so the glossary records that rather than overruling it.

terms.first_use_explanation: Paying to keep function instances warm so the cold start is not on the request path.
A helper process deployed alongside the app to handle a cross-cutting concern.
How long a single call takes end to end.
Where work waits when arrivals outpace service. Depth is the signal, not the symptom.
Sending a failed call again — safe only when the operation is idempotent and the retry is bounded.
The slow end of the latency distribution — p95, p99, p99.9 — which is what real users complain about.
terms.note: `cola` is NOT banned: it is the ordinary word for queue and appears 356 times in that sense.

terms.first_use_explanation: The property that applying an operation twice leaves the same state as applying it once.
Replicas converge, but a read right after a write may not see it.
A complete independent instance of the stack serving a subset of customers, so failure is contained.
How much can be damaged by a single failure or compromise.
Keeping working when the control plane is unavailable, by not needing it to serve.
Adding or removing capacity from a signal — and the delay between the signal and the capacity.
A cap on requests per caller per window, enforced to protect the callee.
terms.note: Thin either way (5 Spanish vs 4 English uses). `límite de tasa` wins narrowly and is unambiguous, which the bare English is not — `rate` alone reads as several things.

terms.first_use_explanation: Moving retries, mTLS and traffic policy out of each app and into the platform layer.
terms.note: Measures as `kept` on 4 English and 2 Spanish uses — too thin to be a signal. `malla de servicios` (3) is the settled Spanish form in the corpus and wins on the Spanish-side count.

terms.first_use_explanation: Being able to answer a new question about production without shipping new code.
Following one request across services, so latency can be attributed rather than guessed.
terms.note: `trazas` (36) clearly beats `tracing` (6) in Spanish prose; the 26 English uses are what make the raw ratio look inconsistent.

terms.first_use_explanation: A target set on an SLI over a window, e.g. 99.9% under 300 ms across 28 days.
A number observed directly about service quality, almost always a ratio of good events to all events.
A contract with the customer plus consequences — credits, penalties — when it is missed.
The gap between the SLO and 100%: at 99.9% you may be unhealthy 0.1% of the window.
terms.note: Both forms ship (67 singular, 2 plural). The singular is canonical; the plural is banned to settle it.

terms.first_use_explanation: The latency the slowest 1% of requests exceed. It degrades under load because queues form.
The latency the slowest 5% of requests exceed.
A short, current doc per alert: what it means, how to confirm it, the first diagnostic steps.
Repetitive manual on-call work that scales with traffic and leaves no durable value.
The research programme that named four delivery metrics separating high from low performers.
Sending a small slice of traffic to the new version and deciding on numbers, not on watching.
terms.note: `canario` (9) is allowed as the adjective the corpus already uses ("lanzamiento canario", "umbral del canario"); the noun is `canary`.

terms.first_use_explanation: Two full environments; the switch is a routing change, so rollback is the same change reversed.
terms.note: `azul-verde` (3) appears as a gloss beside the English term and is left alone.

terms.first_use_explanation: Returning to the last known-good version. The interesting question is whether it is automatic.
terms.note: Also the database sense (a transaction rolling back); the same word covers both here.

terms.first_use_explanation: In a database, the point after which the write survives a crash. In version control, one recorded change.
terms.note: There is a THIRD sense in the corpus — disagree-and-commit, full support for a decision made against you. That one is a verb in prose, not this term, which is why `confirmar` (27 uses) is not banned.

terms.first_use_explanation: A runtime switch that lets unfinished code merge to trunk turned off.
Everyone merges to one branch daily; long-lived branches are the thing being avoided.
terms.note: `basado en trunk` (6 uses) is the hybrid the corpus actually ships; the fully translated form is banned.

terms.first_use_explanation: A systemic control that makes the dangerous action hard or impossible, rather than discouraged.
terms.note: `guardarraíl` (9) is the accepted Spanish spelling and ships; `barandilla` is a handrail. `límite` (230) and `barrera` (29) are NOT banned either: the first means threshold, the second is literal.

terms.first_use_explanation: The supported default path that is easier than the alternatives, so teams choose it without a mandate.
A scheduled rehearsal of a failure, run against production or a faithful copy.
The written account after an incident, whose value is the systemic cause, not the timeline.
Written so the cause is a system property rather than a person's mistake.
terms.note: Both forms ship (31 vs 4); the singular is canonical.

terms.first_use_explanation: The rotation that owns production right now, and is paged when the SLO burns.
terms.note: Spanish says `guardia` / `de guardia` (155) far more than `on-call` (32).

terms.first_use_explanation: Any divergence between declared infrastructure and deployed reality.
The part that decides and configures, as opposed to the part serving requests.
terms.note: `plano de control` (44) beats `control plane` (15) in Spanish prose. The pair with `data plane` is decided together so the two halves cannot drift apart. `capa de control` is NOT banned: its one use describes guardrails as an online control LAYER, which is a different idea from the control plane.

terms.first_use_explanation: The part that actually serves the request path.
terms.note: Follows `control plane`: `plano de datos` (9) against 3 English uses in Spanish prose. `capa de datos` is NOT banned — it means the data tier, a different idea.

terms.first_use_explanation: The pre-built multi-account baseline — identity, network, logging, guardrails — a workload lands in.
terms.note: `zona de aterrizaje` (7) against 2 uses of the English form in Spanish prose.

terms.first_use_explanation: Granting exactly the permissions needed, and nothing that is merely convenient.
terms.note: Three variants ship (23 / 4 / 2). One is canonical and the other two are banned to end the drift.

terms.first_use_explanation: The machine-readable list of what is actually inside a build.
The cost of leaving a vendor, which is a number you can estimate rather than a feeling.
terms.note: `amarre` (19) outnumbers `lock-in` (14) and is deliberately allowed: it is idiomatic and the corpus uses it for exactly this idea ("la ubicación del catálogo decide el amarre"). `bloqueo` (49) is not banned either — it means a database lock here.

terms.first_use_explanation: How much would have to change to run the same workload somewhere else.
terms.note: `portabilidad` (19) against 5 uses of `portability` in Spanish prose — a direct cognate, so there is no reason to keep the English.

terms.first_use_explanation: Billing each team for the infrastructure it consumes, so cost lands where the decision is made.
Cost per unit of value delivered — per request, per tenant — rather than total spend.
One customer's isolated slice of a shared system.
terms.note: Nearly even (78 vs 64), so neither form is banned. `tenant` is canonical for new prose; `inquilino` is correct Spanish and stays. `cliente` (322) means customer and is unrelated.

terms.first_use_explanation: One deployment serving many customers, where isolation is a design property and not a hope.
terms.note: `multi-inquilino` (3) is consistent with `inquilino` staying legal above.

terms.first_use_explanation: The latency half of all requests come in under — the typical case, and the one that hides the problem.
How long a cached value stays valid. Expiry is a failure mode, not a cleanup detail.
terms.note: `tiempo de vida` (7) coexists as a first-use gloss and is not banned.

terms.first_use_explanation: Under a network partition you choose consistency or availability. It says nothing about the normal case.
terms.note: Ratio 0.41 is misleading: the English figure counts `CAP` inside `PACELC` discussions and in "CAP theorem", while Spanish writes `teorema CAP`. The acronym itself is never translated.

terms.first_use_explanation: Extends CAP with the question that matters more day to day: latency or consistency when there is no partition.
The four guarantees a transaction gives, of which durability is the one that survives a crash.
Separating the write model from the read model, which buys read scale and costs you consistency.
Publishing a stream of committed database changes, so downstream systems follow the log rather than poll.
A write-optimised index: buffer in memory, flush sorted runs, merge them later. Writes are cheap, reads pay.
Arrival rate. Compared against service rate, it tells you whether a queue forms.
terms.note: `peticiones por segundo` (14) is a legitimate expansion and stays.

terms.first_use_explanation: How long before the first token appears — a separate serving goal from inter-token latency and throughput.
Scores retrieval by how high the first relevant result lands, averaged over queries.
Data that identifies a person, whose leakage is a compliance event and not just a bug.
The body whose Top 10 lists name the most consequential risks — including one specific to LLM applications.
A threat-modelling checklist applied per trust boundary, which is what makes it exhaustive rather than clever.
One isolated failure domain within a region — the unit multi-AZ redundancy is measured in.
terms.note: Closest call among the acronyms: `zona de disponibilidad` (9) nearly matches `AZ` (13). Both stay.

terms.first_use_explanation: The non-management track, where scope grows through leverage rather than headcount.
What an option gains in exchange for what it gives up; every real alternative has both.
terms.note: `compensación` (61) outnumbers `tradeoff` (36) and is deliberately still allowed — it is idiomatic Spanish. This entry sets the canonical form without invalidating shipped prose.

terms.first_use_explanation: What a piece of work includes and, more usefully, what it excludes.
Output that continues after you stop pushing, because it changed how others work.
The coordination that makes a project land and that no artifact records.
Spending your own credibility to put someone into an opportunity they cannot reach alone.
terms.note: `padrinazgo` (7) is used deliberately alongside `patrocinio` (103) to separate sponsoring a person from sponsoring a project, so it is allowed.

terms.first_use_explanation: Advice given to someone who then decides. Distinct from sponsorship, which spends your capital.
Handing over the decision, not the typing.
Changing what other teams do without authority over them.
Anyone whose work the decision changes, including the people who will operate it.
terms.note: Thin evidence (6 vs 16) and no dominant Spanish form; the English term is standard in the region.

terms.first_use_explanation: A short record of one decision, its context and what it rules out — written when it is made.
A written proposal circulated for comment before the work starts.
The document that makes a design reviewable before it is code.
terms.note: `documento de diseño` leads 42 to 4; the short form is an abbreviation, not a calque.

terms.first_use_explanation: The sequenced plan, whose honest version names what is being deferred.
terms.note: `roadmap` leads 22 to 6, but `hoja de ruta` is standard Spanish and is not worth banning.

terms.first_use_explanation: The role accountable for a team's technical direction and delivery.
terms.note: `líder técnico` is NOT banned. Its uses are inside scenarios ("tu líder técnico eligió el otro enfoque"), where the natural Spanish reads better than the English title; `tech lead` stays canonical for the role name itself.
